--- format: live-html: webr: packages: - survival --- # Time-to-event data and censoring {#sec-survival-data} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In this chapter **The question.** Patients with advanced lung cancer are followed up after joining a study. Some die during follow-up, but many are still alive when the study ends. How can we describe how long these patients survive? **By the end of this chapter you will be able to:** - recognise time-to-event data and its three ingredients: a time origin, an event and a time scale; - explain what **censoring** is, and why ignoring it gives the wrong answer; - state the assumption of **non-informative censoring**; - create a survival outcome in R with `Surv()`. ::: This chapter has your first **live R exercises**: code boxes you can edit and run in the page itself. @sec-live-exercises explains how they work. ## What makes survival data special? In **survival analysis** (also called *time-to-event analysis*), the outcome is the *time until an event happens*. The event might be death, relapse, hospital discharge, injury, or a machine failing. Every observation needs three things: 1. A clear **time origin**. When does the clock start? Diagnosis, randomisation, the start of treatment? 2. A clear **event** definition. 3. A **time scale**. Days, months or years since the origin, or age. What makes this kind of data special is **censoring**. For some people the study ends, or they drop out, *before* we see their event. All we know is that their event time is *longer than* the time we observed. The word comes from *censorship*: like a censor blacking out the rest of a document, the rest of the patient's story is hidden from us. ::: {.callout-important} ## Censoring is not missing data A censored observation still tells us something useful. Suppose a patient was last seen alive and event-free after 2.3 years of follow-up. We don't know when they will die, but we do know they survived at least 2.3 years. Throwing that information away, or treating 2.3 years as if it were the event time, biases the results. Survival methods use exactly what we know, and nothing more. ::: ### Types of censoring All the censoring in this book is **right censoring**: we know the event happened *after* a certain time (to the right of it, on a timeline). It has three common causes: - **Administrative censoring.** The study ends. Patients who joined late are followed for less time. - **Loss to follow-up.** The patient moves away or withdraws. - **Competing events.** The patient dies of something else before the event of interest. Strictly, this isn't censoring at all: someone who has died can never relapse. Treating these deaths as censored is a common mistake (@sec-competing). Kaplan–Meier and Cox methods assume that censoring is **non-informative**. At any time, people who are censored must have the same future risk as people who stay under observation. If the sickest patients drop out because they're sick, this assumption is broken. Chapter 4 has an app that shows what happens then (@sec-informative). ## Why not just use the average time, or logistic regression? - The **mean observed time** is biased downwards, because censored times are shorter than the true event times. - Using the **mean among people who had the event** throws away the censored people. It is biased towards fast events. - **Logistic regression** on "died: yes/no" ignores *when* the event happened. It also mixes up people followed for 1 month with people followed for 5 years. The app below makes this concrete. ## Interactive app: what censoring does {#sec-app-censoring} Each line is a patient. Patients join the study at different times during the *recruitment period*, and the study stops at a fixed calendar date. A filled dot ● is an observed event. A cross ✕ is a censored observation. Tick *Show what we never see* to reveal the true event times hidden by censoring. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {makeRandom, mean, quiz} from "./js/survtools.js" ``` ::: {.app} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof c1Scen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "Short study (2 years)", "No drop-out, 10-year study"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"}) c1P = ({"Default": {}, "Short study (2 years)": {"study": 2}, "No drop-out, 10-year study": {"drop": 0, "study": 10}})[c1Scen] viewof c1 = Inputs.form({ n: Inputs.range([5, 40], {value: c1P.n ?? 20, step: 1, label: "Patients shown"}), accrual: Inputs.range([0, 4], {value: c1P.accrual ?? 2, step: 0.5, label: "Recruitment period (yrs)"}), study: Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: c1P.study ?? 5, step: 0.5, label: "Study length (yrs)"}), median: Inputs.range([0.5, 8], {value: c1P.median ?? 3, step: 0.5, label: "True median survival (yrs)"}), drop: Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: c1P.drop ?? 0.1, step: 0.05, label: "Drop-out rate (per yr)"}), seed: Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: c1P.seed ?? 7, step: 1, label: "Random seed"}) }, {template: formGrid}) formGrid = inputs => html`
${Object.values(inputs)}
` viewof c1view = Inputs.radio(["Calendar time", "Time since entry"], {value: "Calendar time", label: "Time axis"}) viewof c1truth = Inputs.toggle({label: "Show what we never see", value: false}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false function simCensoring(p, n, seed) { const r = makeRandom(seed); const rate = Math.LN2 / p.median; const studyEnd = Math.max(p.study, p.accrual); return Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => { const entry = r.unif() * p.accrual; const tEvent = r.exp(rate); const tDrop = p.drop > 0 ? r.exp(p.drop) : Infinity; const tAdmin = studyEnd - entry; const time = Math.min(tEvent, tDrop, tAdmin); const status = tEvent <= Math.min(tDrop, tAdmin) ? 1 : 0; const reason = status ? "Event" : (tDrop < tAdmin ? "Censored: dropped out" : "Censored: study ended"); return {id: i + 1, entry, tEvent, time, status, reason}; }); } c1data = simCensoring(c1, c1.n, c1.seed) c1big = simCensoring(c1, 5000, c1.seed + 1000) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false { const cal = c1view === "Calendar time"; const studyEnd = Math.max(c1.study, c1.accrual); const d = c1data.map(p => ({...p, x0: cal ? p.entry : 0, x1: cal ? p.entry + p.time : p.time, xt: cal ? p.entry + p.tEvent : p.tEvent})); const hidden = d.filter(p => !p.status); return Plot.plot({ height: 120 + 14 * c1.n, marginLeft: 50, x: {label: cal ? "Calendar time since study opened (years) →" : "Time since patient entered (years) →", domain: [0, Math.max(studyEnd, ...(c1truth ? d.map(p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2)) : [studyEnd]))]}, y: {label: "Patient", tickFormat: d => d, domain: d.map(p => p.id)}, color: {legend: true, domain: ["Event", "Censored: study ended", "Censored: dropped out"], range: ["#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7"]}, marks: [ cal ? Plot.ruleX([studyEnd], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}) : null, cal && c1.accrual > 0 ? Plot.rectX([{x1: 0, x2: c1.accrual}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "#999", fillOpacity: 0.08}) : null, c1truth ? Plot.ruleY(hidden, {y: "id", x1: "x1", x2: p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2), stroke: "#aaa", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}) : null, c1truth ? Plot.dot(hidden, {y: "id", x: p => Math.min(p.xt, studyEnd * 2), stroke: "#aaa", r: 3.5}) : null, Plot.ruleY(d, {y: "id", x1: "x0", x2: "x1", stroke: "reason", strokeWidth: 2.5}), Plot.dot(d.filter(p => p.status), {y: "id", x: "x1", fill: "reason", r: 4.5}), Plot.dot(d.filter(p => !p.status), {y: "id", x: "x1", stroke: "reason", symbol: "times", r: 5, strokeWidth: 2}) ] }); } ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false { const big = c1big; const trueMean = c1.median / Math.LN2; const rows = [ {Quantity: "True mean survival time", Value: trueMean, Comment: "What we want to know"}, {Quantity: "Mean of observed times (ignoring censoring)", Value: mean(big.map(d => d.time)), Comment: "Too low: censored times are cut short"}, {Quantity: "Mean time among those with an event", Value: mean(big.filter(d => d.status).map(d => d.time)) || NaN, Comment: "Too low: long survivors are left out"}, {Quantity: "Proportion censored", Value: mean(big.map(d => 1 - d.status)), Comment: "With these settings, over 5,000 simulated patients"} ]; return Inputs.table(rows, {format: {Value: v => isNaN(v) ? "–" : v.toFixed(2)}, layout: "auto", rows: 5}); } ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Things to try For each one, **predict first**: decide what you expect to see, then pick the scenario and check. Committing to a prediction, even a wrong one, makes the result stick. 1. **Predict:** if every patient's line started at 0, which patients would have the shortest lines? *Then* switch the time axis to **Time since entry**. This is how survival software sees the data. 2. **Predict:** if the study lasts only 2 years, will the two naive averages move closer to the truth or further away? *Then* pick **Short study (2 years)**. 3. **Predict:** what happens to the naive averages when almost no one is censored? *Then* pick **No drop-out, 10-year study**. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Answers: what you should see 1. **Time since entry.** Every line now starts at 0. Patients who joined near the end of the recruitment period have the shortest lines ending in a blue ✕. They were censored early because the study closed, not because of anything about their health. That's why administrative censoring is usually *non-informative*. 2. **Study length 2 years.** Most lines now end in a ✕. With the other settings at their defaults, about 80% of patients are censored. The naive mean falls to about 0.8 years (truth: 4.3), and the mean among those with an event to about 0.6 years. Both get worse the shorter the follow-up. The Kaplan–Meier method (Chapter 2) uses the censored patients properly. 3. **No drop-out, 10-year study.** Only people still alive after 8–10 years are censored, about 13% of patients. The naive mean rises to about 3.8 years, much closer to 4.3. It's still too low, because the few censored patients are the longest survivors. Censoring causes the bias: the less of it there is, the smaller the bias. ::: ## Survival data in R: the `Surv()` object We'll use the `lung` dataset from the **survival** package. It has survival times (in days) for 228 patients with advanced lung cancer. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(survival::lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> inst time status age sex ph.ecog ph.karno pat.karno meal.cal wt.loss #> 1 3 306 2 74 1 1 90 100 1175 NA #> 2 3 455 2 68 1 0 90 90 1225 15 #> 3 3 1010 1 56 1 0 90 90 NA 15 #> 4 5 210 2 57 1 1 90 60 1150 11 #> 5 1 883 2 60 1 0 100 90 NA 0 #> 6 12 1022 1 74 1 1 50 80 513 0 ``` ::: ::: The important columns are `time` (days of follow-up) and `status`. Note that in this dataset `status` is coded **1 = censored, 2 = dead**. R accepts 1/2, but 0/1 or `FALSE/TRUE` are clearer, so we recode. We also turn `sex` into a labelled factor. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lung <- survival::lung |> mutate( status = status - 1, # 0 = censored, 1 = died sex = factor(sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")), time_m = time / 30.44 # follow-up in months ) table(lung$status) # 63 censored, 165 deaths ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> 0 1 #> 63 165 ``` ::: ::: `Surv(time, status)` combines the two columns into one survival outcome. Censored times are printed with a `+`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Surv(lung$time, lung$status)[1:15] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 306 455 1010+ 210 883 1022+ 310 361 218 166 170 654 #> [13] 728 71 567 ``` ::: ::: Almost every survival function in R takes a formula with `Surv()` on the left-hand side, for example: ```r survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung) # Kaplan-Meier, Ch 2 coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung) # Cox model, Ch 3 ``` :::: {.optional} ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Going further (optional): other forms of `Surv()` - `Surv(start, stop, event)`: *counting-process* form. Use it for time-varying covariates and delayed entry (left truncation). - `Surv(time, event, type = "interval")`: interval-censored data, where you only know the event happened between two visits. ::: :::: ### How the live exercises work {#sec-live-exercises} ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## Live R exercises The exercises in this book run **real R inside the web page**. There's nothing to install. - The first time you open a page with exercises, R loads in the background. This takes 10–30 seconds, and it's quicker on later visits. Some exercises also download extra packages the first time you run them, so that first run is slower. - Edit the code in the box, then click **Run Code**. Output and plots appear underneath. - Your answer is **checked automatically**, with feedback. - Stuck? Use **Show Hint** for a nudge, or **Show Solution** for the full answer. **Start Over** resets the code. - Each exercise box starts fresh, with its data already loaded, so you can do them in any order. All of this code also works in RStudio on your own computer (see @sec-setup). ::: ### Practice: fill in the blanks Replace each `______` with the right code, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_surv'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_surv library(survival) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_surv' caption='Practice: a survival outcome in R'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_surv #| caption: "Practice: a survival outcome in R" lung <- survival::lung # Recode status from 1 = censored, 2 = died, to 0/1 lung$status <- lung$______ - 1 # The first 10 survival times Surv(lung$______, lung$______)[1:10] # How many died (1) and how many were censored (0)? table(lung$______) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_surv"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 `status` is the column being recoded. `Surv()` takes the time column first, then the status column. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_surv"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 Every blank is either `time` or `status`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_surv"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r lung <- survival::lung lung$status <- lung$status - 1 Surv(lung$time, lung$status)[1:10] table(lung$status) ``` The censored patients are the ones marked `+`: among the first 10, the 3rd (1010+ days) and the 6th (1022+ days). 165 patients died and 63 were censored. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_surv' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_surv #| check: true env <- .envir_result if (is.null(env$lung) || !identical(env$lung$status, survival::lung$status - 1)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "The recoding isn't right yet: the first blank should make status 0 for censored and 1 for died (lung$status - 1).") } else if (!grepl("Surv\\(\\s*lung\\$time\\s*,\\s*lung\\$status", .user_code)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Surv() takes the follow-up time first, then the status: Surv(lung$time, lung$status).") } else if (!is.table(.result) || !identical(as.vector(.result), c(63L, 165L))) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "The last line should count the recoded status values: table(lung$status).") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! 165 patients died and 63 were censored. Which of the first 10 were censored? (Look for the +.)") } ``` ::: ## Quick quiz {.unnumbered} Choose an answer to each question. You'll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz([ { "q": "A patient joined the study 2 years before it closed and was alive on the closing date. How should their record be entered?", "options": [ "Event at 2 years", "Censored at 2 years", "Excluded, because their outcome is missing", "Censored at the total length of the study" ], "answer": 1, "why": "We know they were event-free for 2 years, and nothing after that. So time = 2, status = 0.", "hints": [ "They didn't have the event, so status must be 0 (censored).", "", "Excluding them throws away 2 years of event-free follow-up and biases survival downwards.", "Time is measured from *their* entry, not from when the study opened." ] }, { "q": "Which of these most clearly breaks the 'non-informative censoring' assumption?", "options": [ "Patients recruited late are followed for less time", "A patient moves abroad for a new job", "Patients withdraw because they become too unwell to attend visits", "The study closes on a fixed date" ], "answer": 2, "why": "Those patients are censored *because* their risk is high. People left in the risk set are healthier than the people who leave it, so survival is overestimated.", "hints": [ "Late recruitment is unrelated to prognosis, so this is fine.", "Moving for a job is (probably) unrelated to the risk of the event.", "", "A fixed closing date is unrelated to any one patient's risk." ] }, { "q": "Why is the average of observed follow-up times a poor estimate of average survival?", "options": [ "It's too high, because long survivors dominate", "It's too low, because censored times are shorter than the true event times", "It's fine as long as the sample is large", "It's only a problem when two events happen at the same time" ], "answer": 1, "why": "Each censored time is a lower bound on the true event time, so averaging them pulls the estimate down. A bigger sample doesn't fix this.", "hints": [ "Look at the app again: the naive means were always *below* the truth.", "", "A bias doesn't shrink with sample size. More data just gives a more precise wrong answer.", "Ties are a minor technical issue. Censoring is the real problem." ] }, { "q": "In survival::lung, status is coded 1/2. After status - 1, what does status = 1 mean?", "options": [ "Censored", "Died", "Lost to follow-up", "Alive at 1 year" ], "answer": 1, "why": "The original coding is 1 = censored, 2 = dead. Subtracting 1 gives the usual 0 = censored, 1 = event.", "hints": [ "Censored becomes 0.", "", "Lost to follow-up is a kind of censoring, which is coded 0.", "status records what happened at the end of follow-up, not at a fixed time." ] } ]) ``` ## Exercise ### Exercise 1.1 *These are live exercises: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used them before.* 1. How many patients in `lung` have a missing value in `ph.ecog` (performance score)? 2. What is the longest follow-up time? Was that patient censored, or did they die? Make this the last line, so it can be checked. 3. Write down, in one sentence, what the "time origin" and "event" are for `lung`. (Hint: the help page, `?lung`, describes the variables.) ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_lung_explore'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_lung_explore library(survival) lung <- survival::lung lung$status <- lung$status - 1 # 0 = censored, 1 = died ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_lung_explore' caption='Exercise 1.1: exploring the lung data'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_lung_explore #| caption: "Exercise 1.1: exploring the lung data" # 1. Number of missing values in ph.ecog # 2. The row with the longest follow-up time: show its time and status (last line) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_lung_explore"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 `is.na()` gives `TRUE` for each missing value, and `sum()` counts the `TRUE`s. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_lung_explore"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 `which.max(lung$time)` gives the row number of the longest time, so `lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")]` shows that row. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_lung_explore"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r sum(is.na(lung$ph.ecog)) lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")] ``` One patient has a missing `ph.ecog`. The longest follow-up is 1022 days, and that patient was **censored** (`status = 0`): they were still alive at their last follow-up. For part 3, `?lung` says time is "survival time in days", measured from enrolment, and the event is death from any cause. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_lung_explore' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_lung_explore #| check: true if (!grepl("is\\.na\\s*\\(\\s*lung\\$ph\\.ecog", .user_code)) { list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "For part 1, count the missing values with sum(is.na(lung$ph.ecog)).") } else if (is.data.frame(.result) && all(c("time", "status") %in% names(.result)) && nrow(.result) == 1 && .result$time == 1022) { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! The longest follow-up is 1022 days, and status = 0, so that patient was censored, not dead. (And one patient has a missing ph.ecog.)") } else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && .result == 1022) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Yes, the longest time is 1022 days. Now show that patient's status too: lung[which.max(lung$time), c('time', 'status')].") } else { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line show the time and status of the patient with the longest follow-up. Try which.max(lung$time).") } ``` ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important icon="false"} ## Key points - Survival data record the **time until an event**. You need a clear time origin, a clear event and a time scale. - A **censored** observation tells us only that the event happened *after* the last follow-up. It isn't missing data. It carries real information. - Ignoring censoring gives the wrong answer: averages of observed times are too low, and yes/no analyses ignore *when* events happen. - Survival methods assume censoring is **non-informative**: people who are censored have the same future risk as those still being followed. - In R, `Surv(time, status)` combines follow-up time and event status (1 = event, 0 = censored). In `lung`, `status` must be recoded from 1/2 to 0/1 first. ::: **Answering the question.** We can't just average the follow-up times, because 63 of the 228 patients were censored, so their follow-up times are shorter than their true survival times. We need a method that uses the information in censored patients correctly. That's the Kaplan–Meier estimator, in the next chapter. ## Further reading All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise. The whole book's reading list, grouped by topic, is in @sec-further-reading. - @clark2003: **Start here.** A clear, non-technical introduction to survival data, censoring and Kaplan–Meier curves, written for clinicians and researchers. - @ucla_survival: Free workshop materials with R code, covering how to set up survival data in R and run first analyses. A useful second explanation alongside this book. - @leung1997: *More advanced.* The different kinds of censoring, and why the non-informative censoring assumption matters. (May need institutional access.)
